fetched_contents.text: Dosing of Enoxaparin in Renal Impairment ---------------------------------------- The authors explore efficacy and safety outcomes in multiple degrees of renal impairment when using FDA-approved dosing regimens for enoxaparin and find that a more multitiered dosing strategy appears to be needed. Keywords: low-molecular-weight heparin, unfractionated heparin, bleeding, enoxaparin, renal impairment, pharmacokinetics, hemodialysis Abstract Objective To review enoxaparin treatment dosing, pharmacokinetics, and clinical outcomes data in patients with renal impairment and to examine the current two-tiered dosing regimen approved by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA). Data Sources A literature search of PubMed (1990–2016) was performed using the search terms low-molecular-weight heparin, unfractionated heparin, bleeding, enoxaparin, renal impairment, pharmacokinetics, and hemodialysis. Study Selection and Data Extraction All studies assessing the pharmacokinetic properties of enoxaparin in patients with renal impairment were evaluated. In addition, all retrospective and prospective studies assessing the safety and efficacy of enoxaparin treatment in this population were evaluated. Data Synthesis Five pharmacokinetic studies evaluated changes in the pharmacokinetics of enoxaparin in patients with renal impairment. In these studies, enoxaparin clearance was reduced by 17% to 44% in patients with mild and moderate renal impairment. Six retrospective studies evaluated the safety of enoxaparin in patients with renal impairment. In one study, patients with moderate renal impairment were at increased risk of bleeding when using the current FDA-approved two-tiered scheme (odds ratio, 4.7; 95% confidence interval, 1.7–13.0; P = 0.002). Another study demonstrated that individualized enoxaparin dosing, when compared to FDA-approved dosing, resulted in a decreased risk of bleeding. Two retrospective studies evaluated efficacy. One of these studies compared reduced-dose enoxaparin with unfractionated heparin; there was a trend toward lower incidences of thromboembolism and 30-day mortality with reduced-dose enoxaparin. Hospital length of stay also decreased with reduced-dosed enoxaparin. Conclusions This paper highlights the differences in the pharmacokinetic properties and safety and efficacy outcomes in multiple degrees of renal impairment when using treatment-dose enoxaparin. Given the literature highlighted in this review, a more multitiered enoxaparin renal dosing strategy—perhaps shifting from the current two-tier approach to at least three or four tiers—should be considered. INTRODUCTION The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approved enoxaparin (Lovenox, Sanofi-Aventis U.S.), a low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH), in 1993. Since then multiple generic versions of the drug have been approved as well.1 In general, LMWH agents have been shown to be noninferior to unfractionated heparin (UFH) for the treatment of deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism, and they have largely replaced UFH in many niches for a variety of practical reasons. LMWHs are fragments of UFH, a heterogeneous mixture of sulfated glycosaminoglycans, and are approximately one-third the molecular weight of UFH.2 Enoxaparin exhibits anticoagulant properties similar to UFH by binding to and accelerating the activity of antithrombin III, which further inactivates thrombin (factor IIa) and factor Xa. However, LMWHs exhibit a much greater and specific effect on factor Xa than on thrombin. This difference is a result of the shorter pentasaccharide structure and smaller molecular size of LMWH, which makes it less likely to form a ternary complex necessary for thrombin inhibition.3 There are distinct advantages to the use of LMWHs instead of UFH. LMWHs have a more predictable anticoagulant response, improved subcutaneous bioavailability, dose-independent clearance, longer biological half-life, and a lower incidence of thrombocytopenia.2 Elimination of LMWHs also differs from UFH in that LMWHs are primarily renally eliminated. In contrast, UFH exhibits saturable and nonsaturable mechanisms and is primarily metabolized in the liver and reticuloendothelial system.4 Given the renal elimination of LMWHs, the 2012 CHEST guidelines on antithrombotic therapy and prevention of thrombosis raise concerns regarding the accumulation of the drug and increased bleeding risks with LMWHs in patients with renal dysfunction.5 Furthermore, the American College of Chest Physicians developed a consensus statement recommending the following approaches to dosing LMWH in chronic kidney disease: The use of UFH is preferred over LMWH. If LMWH is chosen, anti-Xa monitoring and/or dose reduction is recommended, and enoxaparin 1 mg/kg once daily may be given.5 Similarly, enoxaparin prescribing information does not delineate dosing recommendations for patients with a creatinine clearance (CrCl) of 15–29 mL/min compared with those whose CrCl is less than 15 mL/min, thus possibly resulting in apprehension among practitioners about the use of enoxaparin in patients with severe renal impairment.6 As discussed in subsequent portions of this paper, this safety dilemma also extends to patients with moderate renal impairment (CrCl of 30–50 mL/min), who, under the current FDA labeling, are not considered for dose reductions. Why bleeding risk matters and how dose adjustment reduces it

Renal impairment increases bleeding risk with enoxaparin because the drug is primarily eliminated by the kidneys, so impaired renal function can cause accumulation and raise the likelihood of bleeding complications. The evidence says enoxaparin bioaccumulates and causes bleeding if administered in therapeutic doses without dose adjustment to patients with impaired renal function [N2-R2], and that current FDA labeling and CHEST guidelines recommend dose adjustments when CrCl is less than 30 mL/min to reduce the risk of accumulation and bleeding [N1-F2]. Another source notes that enoxaparin clearance was reduced by 17% to 44% in patients with mild and moderate renal impairment, which supports the idea that kidney dysfunction changes how the drug is handled in the body [N1-F2]. In addition, a study found that patients with moderate renal impairment had an increased risk of major hemorrhagic events when using the current FDA-approved dosing scheme [N1-F2], and another found that individualized enoxaparin dosing reduced bleeding risk compared with FDA-approved dosing [N1-F2].

Lower dose helps balance clotting and bleeding risk by reducing the amount of drug in the body, which lowers the chance of excessive anticoagulation and bleeding. The same evidence base supports this: dose adjustments are intended to reduce accumulation and bleeding risk [N1-F2], and one source explicitly states that anti-Xa monitoring and/or dose reduction is recommended for LMWH in renal impairment [N1-F2]. A practical implication is that once-daily dosing may be acceptable for some patients, but the patient’s situation appears to require a lower dose because the physician’s guidance already says enoxaparin prophylaxis generally needs a lower dose than 40 mg once daily in severe renal impairment [N2-R1]. The evidence also says the FDA-approved dosing scheme may not be sufficient for moderate renal impairment, and that a multitiered dosing strategy should be considered [N1-F2].

For the practical comparison between 40 mg once daily and 30 mg once daily, the evidence points to dose adjustment rather than routine use of the standard once-daily prophylaxis. The official dosing instructions say 30 mg subcutaneously once daily for severe renal impairment [N3-F1], and another source says CrCl <30 mL/min is the threshold for reducing enoxaparin to 30 mg once daily [N1-R4]. So in the patient’s case, 40 mg once daily is not the correct standard dose for CrCl 25 mL/min; the evidence supports reducing to 30 mg once daily to minimize bleeding risk [N2-R1][N3-F1]. The broader message is that lower dose helps reduce accumulation and bleeding risk while still trying to maintain enough anticoagulation to prevent thrombosis [N1-F2][N2-R2].

Alternative options or when dose adjustment may not be enough

Other LMWHs or alternatives may be preferred in severe renal impairment, but the evidence suggests they are not a universal substitute and depend on the patient’s situation. One source states that an alternative anticoagulant such as unfractionated heparin may be preferred, especially for individuals with CrCl <30 mL/min, with renal failure, or receiving dialysis [N4-F3]. Another source says selected LMWHs can be used safely in patients with impaired renal function, but caution is still needed [N4-R2]. The same UpToDate source also says LMW heparins with lower renal clearance may be preferred in some cases [N4-F3]. For example, the evidence table in UpToDate notes that dalteparin, tinzaparin, and enoxaparin are all used in renal impairment, but different dose adjustments apply depending on CrCl [N4-F3]. Dalteparin is not available in the US in the same way as enoxaparin, and the evidence suggests caution with tinzaparin in severe renal impairment [N4-F3].

Dose adjustment alone may not be enough when renal function is severely impaired or when there are additional bleeding risks. The evidence explicitly says enoxaparin sodium is not recommended for patients with end-stage renal disease (CrCl <15 mL/min) due to lack of data in this population outside the context of hemodialysis [N5-R4]. It also says that enoxaparin use in patients with moderate renal impairment results in higher drug concentration and that the recommended dose may need adjustment [N5-R5]. In addition, the evidence notes that accumulation may occur with repeated doses, and caution should be used in all patients with renal insufficiency [N4-F3]. This means dose adjustment is not a complete substitute for careful monitoring and may need to be combined with anti-Xa monitoring or other safety measures.

Monitoring and additional precautions may be needed because renal impairment increases the likelihood of bleeding. The evidence says anti-Xa monitoring and/or dose reduction is recommended for LMWH in renal impairment [N1-F2], and that patients should be observed carefully for signs and symptoms of bleeding [N3-F1]. It also notes that hyperkalemia is associated with LMW heparin use in renal insufficiency [N4-F3]. So even when dose adjustment is used, monitoring is an important part of safe management, especially in severe renal impairment. Overall, the evidence suggests that while dose adjustment is usually the main strategy, it may not be sufficient alone in end-stage renal disease or when additional bleeding risks are present, and alternatives like unfractionated heparin may be preferred in those cases [N4-F3][N5-R4].

The guidelines and dosing guidance use a common creatinine clearance threshold: CrCl less than 30 mL/min is the key cutoff for dose adjustment. The evidence says current FDA labeling and CHEST guidelines suggest enoxaparin dose adjustments when CrCl is less than 30 mL/min to reduce the risk of accumulation and bleeding [N1-F2]. Another source states that CrCl <30 mL/min is the threshold for reducing enoxaparin to 30 mg once daily [N1-R4]. A third source explicitly says that enoxaparin prescribing information does not delineate dosing recommendations for patients with CrCl 15–29 mL/min compared with those with CrCl <15 mL/min, which creates uncertainty in severe renal impairment [N1-F2]. That same source also says that patients with moderate renal impairment (CrCl 30–50 mL/min) are not considered for dose reductions under the current FDA labeling [N1-F2].

For severe renal impairment, the recommended dose is 30 mg subcutaneously once daily. Once-daily dosing is acceptable in some settings, but should be changed when renal function is severely impaired.
